note: Relative major and minor as one set of notes with two homes: a two-scales play-along on the neck where the dots stay put and only the home note moves, then the minor home and the major's Do lit on the staff and played on the guitar. The key is now moves (any key), so the title and text name the major key only as {{=key}}, the minor key by where it starts (the 6th note), and a {{?key}} line says what stays the same in another key. The old discovery question is now what to listen for, with a feel to reach in each section.

exercise.title: {{=key}} major and its relative minor, same notes
exercise.why: The relative minor is the major scale played from its 6th note, so the notes stay the same, and the note you come to rest on makes it sound major or minor.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome. Under it is the neck with the notes of {{=key}} major, and the line above the neck names the scale to play now.
For the first four bars, play up from a {{=key}} to the next {{=key}} and back down. For the next four, the line names the minor scale: play the same dots up from its first note, the 6th note of {{=key}} major, and back down.
Practice until you hear each half come to rest on its own home note, while the dots on the neck stay the same.

Tap the lowest ringed {{1}} on the staff below to hear the home note of the minor key. Then tap each note up to the next ringed {{b3}}: the home note of {{=key}} major.
Play the same walk on the guitar, from {{1}} up to {{b3}} and back down to {{1}}.
Practice until {{1}} sounds like home and {{b3}} sounds like a step on the way.
{{?key}}In another key every note moves, and the minor key still starts on the 6th note of the major scale.
